title: Quick Revision: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
subject: Science

bullets: A compass needle is a small bar magnet. Its north-pointing end is the north pole.
Field lines go from N to S outside the magnet and from S to N inside, forming **closed curves**.
Where lines are closer, the field is stronger. **Lines never cross**: a compass can't point two ways at once.
Oersted (1820): a current-carrying wire deflects a compass needle, so **electric current produces a magnetic field**.

table: More current; closer to the wire
Circles near the wire; nearly straight lines at the centre
Like a bar magnet; **uniform** (parallel lines) inside
More turns; more current; a soft iron core

bullets: **Right-hand thumb rule:** thumb along the current; curled fingers show the field direction.
**Electromagnet:** a soft iron core inside a solenoid. Magnetism can be switched on and off, and its strength changed.
Example: current from east to west in an overhead wire. The field is north → south below the wire and south → north above it.
A conductor carrying current in a magnetic field experiences a force. The force is **greatest when the current is perpendicular to the field** and **zero when parallel**.
Reverse the current or the field and the force reverses.
**Fleming's left-hand rule:** forefinger = field, middle finger = current, thumb = force (motion), all at right angles.
Used in electric motors, loudspeakers, microphones and measuring instruments. MRI scans use magnetic fields inside the body.

table: Safety: leaked current goes to earth, preventing shock

bullets: Two circuits: **15 A** for high-power appliances (geyser, AC, heater) and **5 A** for bulbs and fans. All appliances are connected in parallel.
**Short-circuit:** live touches neutral and the current shoots up. **Overloading:** too many appliances on one socket, or a voltage surge.
**Fuse / MCB** breaks the circuit when the current exceeds the safe limit. A fuse is placed in the live wire.
